nginx.conf: # WHO IS ASKING, when the only thing that can reach this container is a proxy.
# Nothing publishes a port for this service: the shared edge proxy reaches it over
# a Docker network and nothing else can. So `$remote_addr` is always the proxy, and
# a rate limit keyed on it would put every visitor in the world into one bucket and
# throttle them as one person. That is a worse bug than the one being fixed.
# The client address therefore comes off `X-Forwarded-For`, and it is trusted ONLY
# from the private ranges Docker hands out, which is the only path that exists.
# `real_ip_recursive` walks past the proxies we trust to the first address we do
# not, which is the visitor.
set_real_ip_from 10.0.0.0/8;
set_real_ip_from 172.16.0.0/12;
set_real_ip_from 192.168.0.0/16;
real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For;
real_ip_recursive on;
# SIGNING IN COSTS THE SERVER A FULL BCRYPT, AND IT COSTS IT EVEN WHEN NO SUCH
# ACCOUNT EXISTS.
# That is on purpose: answering faster for an address nobody has would tell an
# attacker which addresses are real. The price is that an anonymous request is the
# most expensive thing this portal does, measured at 42 ms on a fast desktop and
# more like 60 to 150 ms on the two core machine this runs on. Worse, the hashing
# happens inside a transaction that already holds a row lock, and the pool is ten
# connections, so a few dozen requests a second do not slow down signing in - they
# stop the whole portal, and every other site behind the same edge proxy with it.
# Until this session became reachable from the internet, QA sat behind basic auth
# and the question never arose. Production has no such door, so the limit is here.
# Ten a minute with a burst of five: somebody who mistypes their password five times
# in a row is not stopped, and the account itself locks after ten misses in fifteen
# minutes anyway. 429 rather than nginx's default 503, because the client is being
# asked to slow down and not told the server is broken.
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=signin:10m rate=10r/m;
# AND REGISTERING COSTS MORE THAN SIGNING IN, ON TWO MACHINES INSTEAD OF ONE.
# It is the same bcrypt as above and then a round trip to somebody else's SMTP
# relay on top of it, and like signing in it is anonymous: the only thing an
# attacker needs is the XSRF cookie, which /api/places hands to anybody who asks.
# Measured 14.09.2026 against the real thing, one registration took 5175 ms while
# the relay was slow to answer.
# The transaction no longer waits for the relay, so a slow relay can no longer
# take the database with it - that was the worse half and it is fixed in
# RegistrationApi. What a limit is for is the half no code can fix: this route
# makes the portal SEND A LETTER TO AN ADDRESS THE CALLER NAMES, and a machine
# calling it in a loop is a machine posting mail from us to strangers until the
# relay stops trusting the domain. A blacklisted sender is not a slow portal, it
# is a portal whose members stop receiving anything at all.
# THIS IS NOT the general limit on requests the owner put off, and it is not the
# bot check PDL asks for either - a limit slows a machine down, it cannot tell one
# from a person. It is one route, in the shape the route above it already has.
# ITS OWN ZONE AND NOT `signin`, which would be cheaper and wrong: one bucket for
# both means a burst of registrations spends the allowance that is there so a
# member can get in, and the two have nothing to do with each other.
# Five a minute with a burst of three: registering is a thing a person does once,
# and three in a row covers the one honest case there is - a parent filling the
# form in for his children, one after another, from one address. A fourth waits
# twelve seconds. 429 for the same reason as above.
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=registration:10m rate=5r/m;
limit_req_status 429;
server {
listen 80;
server_name _;
root /usr/share/nginx/html;
index index.html;
# Without this the JSON goes over the wire raw. The result set alone is
# over a megabyte and compresses to roughly a seventh of that, which is the
# difference between a screen that appears and a screen that arrives.
gzip on;
gzip_vary on;
gzip_min_length 1024;
gzip_comp_level 6;
gzip_proxied any;
gzip_types
application/javascript
application/json
application/manifest+json
image/svg+xml
text/css
text/javascript
text/plain
text/xml;
# Hashed asset names, so they can be cached forever. index.html never is,
# or a deploy would leave visitors on the previous version.
location /assets/ {
expires 1y;
add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
# SPA routes: all unknown paths fall back to index.html
location / {
try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
# Signing in, rate limited. An exact match, so it wins over the prefix below
# without depending on the order the two are written in.
location = /api/sign-in {
limit_req zone=signin burst=5 nodelay;
include /etc/nginx/nginx-to-backend.conf;
# Registering, rate limited too, and for the reasons beside its zone above: the
# same bcrypt, a letter to an address the caller names, and nobody signed in.
# An exact match for the same reason as the block above it.
location = /api/registration {
limit_req zone=registration burst=3 nodelay;
include /etc/nginx/nginx-to-backend.conf;
# Everything else the backend answers.
location /api/ {
include /etc/nginx/nginx-to-backend.conf;
nginx-to-backend.conf: # How a request reaches the backend, in one home.
# It lives in its own file because two locations need it: `/api/` for everything,
# and an exact `/api/sign-in` that adds a rate limit. Written twice they would
# drift, and the half that drifts would be the one nobody reads.
# The address is resolved at runtime (Docker DNS) through a variable, so nginx
# starts even when the backend service is not up yet.
Dockerfile: # Shows the development controls: the role switch and the switch that moves the
# day the portal is read as. The QA compose file sets it to 1; production sets
# nothing, and both are then absent from the bundle's behaviour.
